name: Credential and secret-store access
description: Detections for reading the places secrets live: browser password and cookie databases, DPAPI master keys, crypto wallets, LSASS memory and credential files on disk. Nearly every rule here needs an exclusion for the application that legitimately owns the file, which is why the 'none' lists matter as much as the 'all' lists.

rules.title: Non-browser process touching a Chromium password database
rules.description: Chromium browsers keep saved passwords in a SQLite file called 'Login Data', encrypted with a DPAPI-protected key from 'Local State'. An infostealer copies both. The rule excludes the browsers themselves, so what is left is something else reading the vault.
rules.author: BruceEDR
falsePositives: Browser profile backup, migration and sync utilities copy Login Data by design. So does enterprise browser-management tooling and some password-manager import wizards.
Endpoint backup agents that image the whole user profile will read this file on every run; exclude them by process name.

rules.title: Non-browser process touching a browser cookie store
rules.description: Session cookies are more valuable than passwords when MFA is enforced, because they represent an already-authenticated session. Chromium moved the store to Network\Cookies; Firefox uses cookies.sqlite. Both are covered.
rules.author: BruceEDR
falsePositives: Profile backup and browser-migration tools read cookie stores legitimately.
Some web-automation and testing frameworks (Selenium, Playwright harnesses) copy cookie databases between profiles.

rules.title: Access to a Firefox key or logins database
rules.description: key4.db holds the NSS key material that decrypts logins.json. Taking one without the other is useless, so a stealer takes both from every profile directory it can find. cert9.db is included because it sits in the same profile and is commonly swept up.
rules.author: BruceEDR
falsePositives: Firefox profile backup and sync tools, and the Firefox Profile Manager itself when run from a helper, will touch these files.
Password-manager import wizards read logins.json deliberately with the user's consent.

rules.title: Non-browser process reading the Chromium Local State key blob
rules.description: 'Local State' carries the DPAPI-wrapped AES key that decrypts everything in Login Data and the cookie store. Reading it is a stronger signal than reading the databases, because almost nothing but the browser needs it.
rules.author: BruceEDR
falsePositives: Enterprise browser-policy and telemetry agents parse Local State for profile inventory.
Full-profile backup software reads it as part of the user directory.

rules.title: Access to a DPAPI master key file
rules.description: %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Protect\<SID>\ holds the user's DPAPI master keys. Copying them lets an attacker decrypt browser secrets, saved RDP and Wi-Fi credentials offline, on a machine you do not control. The Windows components that use DPAPI go through the API, not the file.
rules.author: BruceEDR
falsePositives: Profile-migration tooling (USMT and its commercial equivalents) copies the Protect directory by design.
Full-disk and profile backup agents will read these files on every pass.

rules.title: Access to a cryptocurrency wallet file or extension store
rules.description: Wallet theft is the single most common monetisation path for commodity infostealers, so wallet paths are worth watching even on machines where nobody admits to holding crypto. Extension wallets live in browser LevelDB directories rather than in a wallet application.
rules.author: BruceEDR
falsePositives: The wallet application itself reads these paths constantly. Add the wallet binaries you actually run to a 'none' clause or to the trust allowlist; the rule cannot exclude every wallet on the market.
Backup software imaging the user profile will read wallet files on every run.

rules.title: Handle opened to LSASS with PROCESS_VM_READ
rules.description:
Reading LSASS memory is how credentials are dumped without dropping a tool on disk. The rule matches on the requested access mask carrying PROCESS_VM_READ rather than on any particular dumper, so it does not care whether the caller was MiniDumpWriteDump, comsvcs.dll or bespoke code.

LIMITATION: identifying the target as LSASS depends on the ProcessAccess monitor putting the target image name into the signal's 'detail' field. If your telemetry source does not populate it, this rule cannot fire, and the pid-only fallback below is what you get.
rules.author: BruceEDR
falsePositives: Antivirus and EDR agents (including Microsoft Defender's MsMpEng.exe), Windows Error Reporting, Task Manager and process-inspection utilities such as Process Explorer legitimately open LSASS with read access. The exclusion list covers the common Microsoft ones only; add your own security stack.
A memory-forensics or crash-dump collection tool run by an administrator is indistinguishable from a credential dump at this layer.

rules.title: Handle opened to LSASS with write or thread-creation access
rules.description: Requesting PROCESS_VM_WRITE or PROCESS_CREATE_THREAD on LSASS is not credential reading, it is tampering: patching the process, installing an SSP, or injecting into the one process that must stay trustworthy. There is no benign administrative reason for it.
rules.author: BruceEDR
falsePositives: Some security products inject a monitoring DLL into LSASS to observe authentication. If yours does, it will fire this rule on every boot; exclude it by name after verifying the signature.

rules.title: SAM, SECURITY or SYSTEM hive saved to a file
rules.description: reg save of the SAM and SYSTEM hives yields offline-crackable local password hashes without ever touching LSASS, which is why it survives most LSASS-focused protections. The SYSTEM hive is required to decrypt SAM, so the pair usually appears within seconds of each other.
rules.author: BruceEDR
falsePositives: Incident responders and forensic imaging scripts do exactly this on purpose. Backup tooling for domain controllers may also export SYSTEM.

rules.title: Access to the Active Directory database file
rules.description: ntds.dit is the entire domain's credential material. On a domain controller its only legitimate readers are the directory service and a backup agent; anywhere else on the network it should not exist at all, and a copy in a staging directory is a domain compromise.
rules.author: BruceEDR
falsePositives: Domain-controller backup and disaster-recovery tooling creates IFM media and shadow copies legitimately; those runs are scheduled, so an unscheduled one is the interesting case.

rules.title: Access to a well-known plaintext credential file
rules.description: Cloud CLI tokens, SSH private keys, unattended-install answer files and saved RDP credentials are all secrets that sit in predictable paths in plaintext or reversibly encoded form. Collecting them needs no exploit at all, only file reads.
rules.author: BruceEDR
falsePositives: Developer tooling reads .aws/credentials, .kube/config and .docker/config on every command; on an engineering workstation this rule is close to pure noise and should be scoped or scored down.
Deployment and imaging systems read unattend.xml legitimately during provisioning.

rules.title: Built-in credential enumeration utility executed
rules.description: cmdkey /list and vaultcmd /listcreds enumerate the Windows Credential Manager without any exploit. They are a common early discovery step because they reveal which remote systems the user has saved credentials for.
rules.author: BruceEDR
falsePositives: Administrators and helpdesk scripts run cmdkey /list when troubleshooting saved credentials, and some logon scripts enumerate before adding an entry.

rules.title: Script body wires up keyboard capture APIs
rules.description: SetWindowsHookEx with WH_KEYBOARD_LL, or a polling loop on GetAsyncKeyState, is keylogging. Seeing it in a script body rather than a compiled binary usually means a commodity stealer rather than bespoke tooling.
rules.author: BruceEDR
falsePositives: Legitimate hotkey managers, accessibility software and macro/automation tools (AutoHotkey-style scripts in particular) use exactly these APIs. Intent is not visible at this layer.

rules.title: Access to a chat application token store
rules.description: Discord, Slack and Telegram keep session tokens in LevelDB directories under AppData. A token is a bearer credential: stealing it bypasses both the password and the second factor, which makes these directories a standard stealer target.
rules.author: BruceEDR
falsePositives: The chat clients themselves and their updaters rewrite these directories constantly; the exclusion list covers the common binaries but not every fork or portable build.
Profile backup software will sweep them up along with the rest of AppData.
